Recapitulation, or progressive parallelism, reads the seals, trumpets and bowls as three views of the same period, each ending at the final judgment and each more intense than the last. Its roots are in Victorinus, Tyconius and Augustine. It is common among amillennial and idealist readers (Hendriksen, Beale), and many preterists and historic premillennialists hold a partial version.

The sequential (telescoping) reading takes the seventh seal as opening the trumpets and the seventh trumpet as opening the bowls, so the judgments follow one another in time. It is common among futurists (Walvoord, Thomas) and classic historicists (Elliott). Many sequential readers allow some overlap.

Souls under the altar; the first resurrection

Where the sacrifice was made. This view reads it as the cross, where the old life is laid down. The souls under the altar and the souls "beheaded" in chapter 20 are those who have lost their old head at the cross and now live and reign with Christ.
The sea of glass before the throne

The basin where priests washed. In Revelation it has become a sea of glass, still and clear, and the overcomers stand on it. On this reading the washing by the word is complete, and the believer stands in it rather than striving for it.
Christ among the seven golden lampstands
The only light in the holy place. The lampstands are the churches, and Christ walks among them as priest, trimming the lamps. The light of the sanctuary is Christ shining through his people.
Bread kept before God’s face. The overcomer is promised hidden manna: Christ the bread from heaven, fed on inwardly, not earned.
Golden censer and the prayers of the saints
Incense rose before the veil. In chapter 8 the prayers of the saints rise with incense, and fire from the altar is thrown to the earth: prayer that is answered with the trumpets’ wake-up calls.
The ark seen in the opened temple

Behind the veil, the mercy seat. At the seventh trumpet the temple opens and the ark is seen; by chapter 21 there is no temple, because God and the Lamb are its temple. The veil is gone and the whole city is the most holy place.

Who Is the Rich Man That Shall Be Saved? (Quis dives salvetur), esp. 42

Homily on Mark 10:17-31 closing with the story of the aged apostle John, back from Patmos 'after the tyrant's death', reclaiming a young man who had become a robber chief. Quoted by Eusebius, Church History 3.23.
The oldest surviving Latin commentary on Revelation; says John saw the visions while condemned to the mines of Patmos by Domitian (on 10:11) and identifies the king who 'is' in 17:10 with Domitian.
On Illustrious Men (De viris illustribus), esp. 9 on John
Catalogue of Christian writers; dates John's banishment to Patmos and the writing of the Apocalypse to the fourteenth year of Domitian and his return to Ephesus under Nerva.
Treatise on virginity and asceticism; in 1.26 it reports Tertullian's account of John being cast into boiling oil at Rome and attributes the act to Nero.
Argues that the apostolic churches hold the true faith; chapter 36 lists Rome's glories, including John plunged unhurt into boiling oil and then sent to his island exile.
Defence of Christians addressed to Roman governors; chapter 5 names Nero as the first persecutor and Domitian as 'a portion of Nero in cruelty' who soon stopped and recalled those he had banished.
Origen's commentary on Matthew; on the cup of James and John he says 'the king of the Romans, as tradition teaches' condemned John to Patmos, without naming the emperor.

Early list of New Testament books; says Paul, 'following the order of his predecessor John', wrote to seven churches by name, and that John in the Apocalypse writes to seven churches yet speaks to all.
Panarion (Medicine Chest against Heresies), esp. 51.12 and 51.33
Catalogue and refutation of eighty heresies; in the section on the Alogi it twice places John's prophesying on Patmos in the time of Claudius Caesar.
Letter of the bishop of Smyrna to the church at Philippi; 11.3 (extant in Latin) says Paul boasted of the Philippians in the churches 'which alone then knew the Lord, for we had not yet known him'.
